$comment: THE KERNEL↔COMPANION WIRE CONTRACT for `device.execute`.
This file is the single declaration of which params each `com.aster` companion
action accepts, and which result fields the kernel is allowed to depend on.
It exists because the transport is untyped in BOTH directions: the kernel ships
an opaque `serde_json::Value` (cortex-tools-screen/src/transport.rs) and the
companion parses it into an untyped map where every handler does
`params?.get("someKey") ?: default`. An unknown key was never an error — it was
silently dropped and the action ran with a default. That is how `screen_gesture`
came to be entirely dead, how scroll-to-find degraded to a single swipe, and how
`wait_for {view_id}` hard-failed on every call.
TWO-SIDED ENFORCEMENT — neither side may drift from this file:
aster-one : crates/cortex-tools-screen/src/wire_contract.rs drives every
`screen_*` tool through a recording client and asserts that every
key it puts on the wire appears in `params` below.
aster-mcp : app/src/test/java/com/aster/service/wire/WireContractTest.kt reads
its own copy of this file and asserts each action's handler really
reads those params.
`contract_version` is compiled into both tests. Changing the contract therefore
requires touching BOTH repositories — that friction is the point, because the two
APKs are sideloaded independently and update out of step.
Note on casing: params are declared in the kernel's canonical snake_case. Both
sides widen every key to snake_case AND camelCase on the wire
(`transport::widen_param_casing`, `WireParams.normalize`), so a handler reading
either convention resolves. Do NOT add both spellings here.

observe.$note: `window` is declared by the kernel's tool schema and advertised to the model, but no companion handler reads it — the observe walk always covers every window. Either implement it or drop it from observe.rs's schema.
$invariants: `elements` MUST be returned in reading order (the companion's traversal order,
ascending down the screen) — NOT in rank order. ScreenObserver ranks candidates
to decide WHAT survives the element budget, then re-sorts the survivors by
traversal order before emitting, and `e<N>` refs are assigned from that final
This was an incidental nicety until ordinal resolution shipped. A step may now
declare `ordinal: first | last | <n>` to pick among rows that no primitive can
tell apart (a list of ride options differing only by a fare), and the kernel
indexes the matching peers IN THE ORDER THE COMPANION SENT THEM. If the
companion ever emitted rank order instead, `"the first ride option"` would
silently mean `"whichever row scored highest"` — a wrong tap that reports

take_screenshot.$note: P3: the companion now DERIVES `marks` from its own SnapshotCache when `annotate:true` and none are supplied (optionally pinned by `from_snapshot`). `marks` stays accepted so a caller that has already computed boxes can still send them; the kernel never does.

input_gesture.$note: The kernel's model-facing arg is `type`; gesture.rs renames it to `gesture_type` at dispatch because `type` has no casing alias.

wait_for.$note: `ok` mirrors `matched` so a TIMEOUT reads as failure through result_failed().

screen_prompt.$note: `text_input` is accepted by InteractiveOverlayModel.parsePrompt but the kernel's screen_prompt tool never sends it.

screen_set_policy.$note: Owner allow/deny push (screen:set-app-policy fan-out + screen:sync-app-policy on companion connect). A WHOLE-POLICY replace, not a merge: a package the owner cleared must disappear companion-side, so an absent key means the empty set. Not a `screen_*` TOOL — dispatched by the RPC handler, so the kernel's drive_all() fixture does not exercise it.
